reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A common overuse injury causing lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists
Pain localises over the lateral femoral epicondyle and is provoked by repetitive flexion and extension, characteristically near thirty degrees of flexion
The Noble compression test and the Ober test for iliotibial band tightness assist the diagnosis
Contributing factors include training errors, downhill running, worn footwear, hip abductor weakness and lower-limb malalignment such as genu varum
Rather than a true friction phenomenon, current understanding attributes the pain to compression of a richly innervated fat pad beneath the band
There is point tenderness over the lateral femoral epicondyle without a joint effusion
It should be distinguished from lateral meniscal and patellofemoral pathology
Generic management includes relative rest and activity modification, stretching with hip abductor strengthening, corticosteroid injection and, rarely, surgical release or lengthening
reference.pathophysiology: Iliotibial band syndrome arises when repetitive knee flexion and extension causes the distal iliotibial band to compress the underlying highly vascular and innervated connective and fatty tissue against the lateral femoral epicondyle, particularly around thirty degrees of flexion. This produces local inflammation and pain. Hip abductor weakness, training overload, downhill running and lower-limb malalignment predispose to the condition. It was historically attributed to friction of the band moving back and forth over the epicondyle.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination including the Noble compression and Ober tests with point tenderness over the epicondyle
MRI showing a thickened band with fluid or oedema beneath it when the diagnosis is uncertain
Ultrasound to assess the band and underlying tissue
Plain radiographs to exclude joint pathology and assess alignment
Gait and biomechanical assessment to identify predisposing factors
redFlags: True mechanical symptoms such as locking suggesting a meniscal or intra-articular lesion
A joint effusion pointing to an intra-articular cause
Neurological symptoms suggesting common peroneal nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good with conservative management and correction of training and biomechanical factors, though the condition tends to recur if these factors are left unaddressed.
pitfalls: Missing intra-articular pathology, signalled by an effusion or locking
Ignoring hip abductor weakness and biomechanical factors, leading to recurrence
Prescribing prolonged rest without addressing the underlying cause
Relying on stretching alone without strengthening
management: Reduce the aggravating load with relative rest, decreased mileage and avoidance of downhill running
Refer for physiotherapy focused on hip abductor strengthening and correction of lower-limb biomechanics
Control acute pain with ice and a short course of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Offer a local corticosteroid injection beneath the band for persistent lateral epicondylar pain
Correct predisposing factors including worn footwear and malalignment, using orthoses where appropriate
Reserve surgical release or lengthening of the band for the uncommon refractory case after failed conservative care

Locking, effusion, neurological symptoms or night pain?

Noble and Ober tests, radiographs, MRI if uncertain, gait assessment
